t: Reading one person's whole genome cost a hundred million dollars in 2001. It now costs about two hundred.
The first human genome cost roughly $100 million and took over a decade. The same read now costs a couple of hundred dollars and takes about a day.
sub: That is a bigger fall than computers managed over the same years.
Half a million-fold, against roughly two thousand-fold for computing power. It is the fastest-falling cost in the history of measurement.

question: What changes when reading a genome becomes cheap?
What follows from sequencing cost falling by five orders of magnitude?
options: You stop asking one question and start reading everything
Nothing much — it is the same information
stages.outcome: You stop asking one question and start reading everything
note: Commit. Ask what you would do differently if a measurement went from unaffordable to trivial.

stages.label: What it cost to read one genome
captions: 2001: $100,000,000. One genome, thirteen years, an international consortium.
2007: $10,000,000. Still a research project in its own right.
2015: $1,500. Cheap enough to sequence a patient.
2023: about $200. Cheap enough to sequence a sample you are merely curious about.
t: Watch what a genome cost to read, year by year.
Follow the cost curve, and note where the qualitative change happens — it is not where the cost is lowest, but where it stops being a reason not to.
after: Once it is cheap, you sequence first and think afterwards. That changes what questions are askable.
The threshold that matters is where cost stops determining what gets measured. Below that, whole categories of question become answerable — including ones nobody would have proposed at the old price.

t: Working out the order of the letters is called sequencing.
Sequencing determines the order of bases. Modern methods read enormous numbers of short fragments in parallel and reassemble them computationally.
High-throughput sequencing reads millions of short fragments simultaneously; the assembly is a computational problem, which is why the field became as much bioinformatics as biology.

The shift from reading one sequence carefully to reading everything and sorting it out afterwards changed what biology is like to do. It also created a durable asymmetry: sequences accumulate far faster than anyone can work out what they do, so the bottleneck moved from data to interpretation and has stayed there.
sub: You do not read it in one go. You read millions of tiny pieces and fit them together.
The fragments overlap, and overlapping is what lets software reconstruct the order.
It also removed the requirement to grow anything, which is what opened up the microbial world you could not culture.

Metagenomics — sequencing everything in a sample without isolating anything — revealed whole branches of life that a century of culturing had missed entirely. That is the same lesson as the microscope, one level along: the instrument decided what was knowable, and the limit was invisible from inside.

q: What is the hard part now that sequencing is cheap?
Why did cheap sequencing not resolve the interpretation problem?
options: Working out what any of it means
Nothing — it is a solved problem
why: Reading the letters is now easy. Knowing what a particular change does to a person is not, and mostly we still cannot say.
Data generation outran interpretation. Most human genetic variants found in a clinical test are classed as of uncertain significance — the sequence is known and its consequence is not.

Because cost was never the limiting factor on understanding. Sequencing tells you the letters; connecting a variant to a phenotype requires population data, functional work and statistics, none of which got cheaper at the same rate. The gap has widened rather than closed, which is a general pattern when one step in a pipeline improves by orders of magnitude and the others do not.

t: A new virus can now be read within days of anyone noticing it.

The SARS-CoV-2 genome was sequenced and published within weeks of the first cases, and vaccine design began from that sequence alone — before anyone had the virus in most laboratories. The speed came directly from this cost curve, and it is the clearest case of a measurement becoming cheap enough to change what is possible rather than merely what is convenient.
